opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to one simple belief: in this field, you can't make good decisions if you lose touch with the details. AI research moves incredibly fast. A paper that looks great on paper might hide a subtle bug in the data pipeline, or a design choice that quietly limits how far the approach can scale. If I only look at slides and summaries, I'm making judgments based on a compressed, filtered version of reality. And when you're deciding where a team of researchers should spend the next year, that compression can be very costly.

There's also a practical side. When I read code, I understand what's actually hard. Sometimes a researcher tells me a problem is nearly solved, and when you look closely, the remaining ten percent is where all the real difficulty lives. Other times something sounds impossible, but the code shows there's a clean path forward. Being close to the implementation helps me calibrate, so I can push where pushing makes sense and be patient where patience is needed.

And honestly, I just enjoy it. I started as a researcher, and I still think of myself as one. Building things, debugging, seeing a model finally train properly, that's the part of the job that gives me energy. If I stepped away from it completely, I think I'd gradually lose my intuition, and intuition is really the core asset for anyone leading research. So reviewing code isn't a distraction from my job as a VP. In many ways, it is the job. It keeps me honest, it keeps me credible with the team, and it keeps me learning.

r001.rationale: He says that staying close to implementation preserves his intuition and keeps him from losing touch with the details needed to make research decisions as a VP.

r002.rationale: He explains that reading code helps him see what is difficult and calibrate how to respond, but does not connect understanding technical pain points to understanding each person’s contribution.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's the only way I know how to do the job. When you become a VP, people assume you stop touching code, that you just go to meetings and make decisions based on slides. But a slide is a very lossy compression of what's actually happening. If I only look at the summary, I'm trusting that whoever made the summary understood the problem correctly, understood what mattered, and had the time to figure that out. Very often that's not the case, not because people are careless, but because the interesting details are exactly the ones that are hard to put on a slide.

So when I read a pull request, or when I ask to see the training config, or how the data loader actually samples, I'm not checking on people. I'm trying to build my own picture of the system so that when I make a decision, it's grounded in something real. Many of the biggest mistakes I've seen in research organizations came from a leader who had a mental model of the system that was two or three versions out of date. They approved a direction that was already impossible, or they killed something that was actually working, because nobody told them the thing that had changed.

There's another reason, which is more personal. I came up as a researcher. I like the details. If you take that away from me, I'm not sure what I'm good at anymore. The moment I stop understanding the code, my judgment starts to drift, and then my only tool is to repeat what other people tell me. I think that's a dangerous place for a technical leader to be.

And frankly, the field is moving too fast. The way we train a world model today is quite different from two years ago. If I don't go into the details, I can't tell the difference between a real breakthrough and a nicely written report. The team knows I read the code, so the conversations become more honest. People bring me the real problems instead of the polished version. That alone is worth the time.

r001.rationale: Liu says that reviewing code and technical details keeps his mental model current and grounds his decisions in the real system, avoiding the drift that comes from relying only on summaries as a leader.

r002.rationale: The response says technical detail helps him understand system problems and hear the team’s real issues, but it does not connect understanding technical pain points to understanding each person’s contribution.

astra-6.text:
For me, staying close to the technical details is part of being useful as a research leader. If I only look at slides or final results, I can miss the assumptions behind them. Reading the code helps me understand what actually works, what is still fragile, and where the team is getting stuck.

It also makes the conversation with researchers much more concrete. I can ask better questions and help think through a problem. Of course, I have to be careful not to become a bottleneck or make every technical decision myself. The goal is to understand enough to support the team and exercise good judgment. And I still enjoy the technical work—that curiosity doesn’t disappear when your title changes.

r001.rationale: He says code review helps him see what works, what is fragile, and where the team is stuck, and that he needs this understanding to support the team as a research leader.

r002.rationale: He says technical understanding helps him ask better questions and support researchers, but does not connect understanding project pain points to understanding each person’s contribution.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, reviewing code is a way to stay close to the research. A high-level presentation can make an idea sound very convincing, but the implementation reveals the assumptions, the trade-offs, and where things actually break.

As a research VP, I need that understanding to make useful decisions. If someone is facing a technical challenge, I want to be able to ask good questions and help them think it through. It also keeps me learning from the team. The further your role moves from day-to-day research, the more intentional you have to be about maintaining that connection.

r001.rationale: The response says code review keeps Liu close to research and that he must intentionally maintain that connection as his role moves away from day-to-day research.

r002.rationale: The response connects technical understanding to making decisions and helping with challenges, but does not say it is needed to understand each person’s contribution to a project.
